newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA ROMTELECOM TO SELL 30 PCT STAKE BY MID-1998.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA ROMTELECOM TO SELL 30 PCT STAKE BY MID-1998.

text.p: Romania will choose an investor to purchase a 30 percent stake in the state-run Romtelecom RA by mid-1998, in a first move to privatise the telephone operator, a top government official said on Friday.
"The ideal candidate should be a consortium of firms combining an operator's expertise with money," Communications Ministry State Secretary Dumitru Moinescu told Reuters.
Moinescu said the ministry had appointed last week investment bank Goldman Sachs as adviser for Romtelecom's privatisation and that a contract with the bank was expected to be signed next month.

Under the arrangement, Goldman Sachs will manage the bid for Romtelecom's privatisation, which would be preceded by the transformation of Romtelecom into a state-owned joint-stock company of "national interest" next month.
"Our plan is to sell initially a 30 percent stake in Romtelecom," Moinescu said, adding that the ministry had already received offers from big Western telecoms firms.
The remaining 70 percent would be offered through the Bucharest stock exchange and in over-the-counter-trading "in order to diminish the state's influence gradually".
The governement would retain a golden share, to intervene in case the new company "ran counter to the national interests", Moinescu said.
With the privatisation, Romania is hoping to improve its teledensity, at 14 percent among the lowest in Europe.

Romania's privatisation programme, launched in 1995 after long delays, has so far failed to deal with large utilities, including Romtelecom, which form the core of the economy and offer the best hope of attracting big foreign investment.
"We evaluate Romtelecom's assets and the market it could offer at around $6 billion. So we expect handsome returns from its privatisation," Moinescu said.
Romtelecom has a monopoly on telephone services, employs 55,000 people and has some 2.8 million subscribers.
Moinescu said the company would also launch a restructuring programme, including upgrading of Romtelecom's infrastructure to raise its market value ahead of privatisation.
Under the plan, some 500,000 new lines would be installed by the end of 1997. Wireless systems are also considered for remote areas to replace expensive landlines, he said.
In March, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development signed a letter of intent to give Romtelecom a $200 million loan to fund its development and privatisation plans.
In 1992 the EBRD gave Romtelecom a credit of 142 million ECUs to install a fibre optic telecommunications network.
